claims.text: Traditional fusion-welding repair is ineffective for the specified high-chromium martensitic stainless steel or similar alloy because of hot-cracking risk.
TLP bonding with a thin boron- or silicon-containing low-melting interlayer can repair the damaged component.
The TLP repair thermal cycle reaches a peak temperature of 1000–1100°C.
The TLP process avoids bulk melting of the base material.
Holding at the peak temperature enables isothermal solidification of the transient liquid layer.
TLP bonding produces a diffusion-bonded interface.
The bonded interface has a graded compositional transition from the interlayer to the base material.
The graded interface reduces residual stresses.
The graded interface reduces interfacial discontinuities.
A short-lived liquid forms at the interface and permits interdiffusion between the interlayer and base material.
Interdiffusion followed by isothermal solidification produces the graded bond.
Avoiding the rapid, uncontrolled solidification associated with fusion welding mitigates hot cracking.
TLP-bonded repairs will have greater resistance to crack initiation under severe mechanical and thermal loads than fusion-welded repairs.
TLP-bonded repairs will have greater resistance to crack propagation under severe mechanical and thermal loads than fusion-welded repairs.
TLP-bonded repairs will exhibit better microstructural homogeneity than traditional fusion-welded repairs.
Traditional fusion-welding repairs typically suffer hot cracking because they fully melt and resolidify the material.
The repair is applicable to components whose operating peak temperatures are around 1000–1100°C.
Interlayer composition and process-control variability may affect repair consistency.
